definition: Case-based reasoning (CBR), broadly construed, is the process of solving new problems based on the solutions of similar past problems.
details: In everyday life, an auto mechanic who fixes an engine by recalling another car that exhibited similar symptoms is using case-based reasoning. A lawyer who advocates a particular outcome in a trial based on legal precedents or a judge who creates case law is using case-based reasoning. So, too, an engineer copying working elements of nature (practicing biomimicry) is treating nature as a database of solutions to problems. Case-based reasoning is a prominent type of analogy solution making. It has been argued that case-based reasoning is not only a powerful method for computer reasoning, but also a pervasive behavior in everyday human problem solving; or, more radically, that all reasoning is based on past cases personally experienced. This view is related to prototype theory, which is most deeply explored in cognitive science.

explainer.lead: Case-based reasoning solves a new problem by looking for similar problems from the past and reusing what worked for them. It matters because this kind of analogy appears in everyday human judgment as well as in computer reasoning.

tiers.eli5: Imagine your bike makes a strange noise, and you remember that a similar noise once meant a loose part. You check that part first instead of starting from nothing. Case-based reasoning is solving today’s problem by learning from a similar problem you have already solved.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer applying case-based reasoning needs past problems paired with their solutions and a way to judge which cases resemble the current problem. The earlier solution can then be reused or adapted rather than constructed from scratch. A poor match can transfer an unsuitable solution, so similarity to the new problem is central.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation: given a new problem p and past cases (q, s), where q is a problem and s its solution, select a case whose q is similar to p and base a solution for p on s. This broad formulation does not specify a representation or similarity measure. Case-based reasoning is a prominent form of analogical problem solving and has also been proposed as a pervasive feature of human reasoning, in a view related to prototype theory.

explainer.example: A mechanic is trying to fix an engine and recalls another car that showed similar symptoms. The mechanic uses the repair that worked on that car as the basis for fixing this one, adapting it to the current vehicle.

usedIn.name: Auto repair
usedIn.detail: A mechanic recalls a car with similar engine symptoms and uses its successful repair as a starting point.

usedIn.name: Legal reasoning
usedIn.detail: Lawyers argue from legal precedents, while judges create case law through decisions in particular cases.

usedIn.name: Biomimetic engineering
usedIn.detail: Engineers copy working elements of nature, treating nature as a collection of solutions to problems.

explainer.intuition: Experience is useful because a new situation often resembles an earlier one. Instead of solving every problem from first principles, case-based reasoning finds a relevant past experience and builds on its solution.
howItWorks: Start with the new problem that needs a solution.
Compare it with past problems that have known solutions.
Select a past case with relevant similarities.
Reuse or adapt that case’s solution for the new problem.
explainer.whyItMatters: Case-based reasoning offers computers a way to draw on concrete experience rather than relying only on general rules. It also describes a familiar pattern of human problem solving, from mechanical diagnosis to legal argument.
misconceptions: The new problem does not have to be an exact repeat; useful cases can be similar rather than identical.
It is not exclusively a computer technique: recalling precedents and personal experiences are everyday forms of the same idea.
It is not limited to artificial intelligence research, since the same pattern appears in law, repair work, and engineering.
